chief_complaint: overwhelming urge to move my legs and crawling sensations in calves every evening
hpi_details: 1-year history of an irresistible, intense urge to move both legs, accompanied by deeply uncomfortable sensations inside his calves and thighs described as 'creeping, crawling, fizzy, or worms wiggling under the skin.' Symptoms exhibit strict circadian and rest dependency: they begin reliably every evening between 8 PM and 10 PM whenever he sits still watching TV or lies down in bed attempting to sleep. The uncomfortable crawling sensation is temporarily relieved within seconds by getting up and pacing around the bedroom or vigorously stretching his legs, but returns within minutes of lying back down. Resulting severe onset insomnia has caused profound daytime fatigue and irritability. Wife reports he kicks and twitches his legs repetitively while sleeping (Periodic Limb Movements of Sleep - PLMS). Has donated whole blood every 3 months for the past 4 years.
ideas: thinks he has poor circulation or restless leg veins caused by sitting at an office desk all day
concerns: exhausted from getting only 3 hours of fragmented sleep per night, affecting his ability to drive safely
expectations: wants sleeping pills or circulation tablets to stop the leg crawling and let him sleep through the night
pmh: regular blood donor (4x/year for 4 years), mild gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
medications: omeprazole 20mg OD, occasional over-the-counter diphenhydramine (antihistamine) for sleep which made the leg restlessness dramatically worse
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks 2 cups of coffee in late afternoon, software manager, married

clinical_knowledge.topic: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom Disease) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom Disease) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management includes reviewing potentially exacerbating medicines; stop over-the-counter diphenhydramine and discuss changes to prescribed medicines with the prescriber, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: overwhelming urge to move my legs and crawling sensations in calves every evening

Key HPI features: 1-year history of an irresistible, intense urge to move both legs, accompanied by deeply uncomfortable sensations inside his calves and thighs described as 'creeping, crawling, fizzy, or worms wiggling under the skin.' Symptoms exhibit strict circadian and rest dependency: they begin reliably every evening between 8 PM and 10 PM whenever he sits still watching TV or lies down in bed attempting to sleep. The uncomfortable crawling sensation is temporarily relieved within seconds by getting up and pacing around the bedroom or vigorously stretching his legs, but returns within minutes of lying back down. Resulting severe onset insomnia has caused profound daytime fatigue and irritability. Wife reports he kicks and twitches his legs repetitively while sleeping (Periodic Limb Movements of Sleep - PLMS). Has donated whole blood every 3 months for the past 4 years.

Objective/Exam findings: Neurological and vascular examination during daytime clinic: completely normal peripheral pulses, reflexes, sensation, and motor power (normal examination between evening attacks confirms primary RLS). Bloods: CRITICAL SCREENING for iron stores: check serum ferritin, iron panel, transferrin saturation, and FBC (ferritin <75 ug/L or transferrin saturation <20% strongly exacerbates central dopaminergic dysfunction in RLS even in the absence of overt anaemia; patient's regular blood donations cause depleted iron stores). Check U&Es (rule out uraemic RLS) and fasting glucose (peripheral neuropathy screen).
Relevant background/PMH: regular blood donor (4x/year for 4 years), mild gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
Current medications: omeprazole 20mg OD, occasional over-the-counter diphenhydramine (antihistamine) for sleep which made the leg restlessness dramatically worse
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom Disease).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peripheral neuropathy (continuous, not evening-dependent) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: constant, not evening-predominant, sensory symptoms, motor weakness or muscle wasting on exam, or severe or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia.
management_principles: Review potentially exacerbating medications: stop over-the-counter diphenhydramine and discuss changes to prescribed medicines with the prescriber

Iron replenishment therapy: initiate oral ferrous sulphate 325mg OD (or ferrous bisglycinate) taken with Vitamin C on an empty stomach if ferritin <75 ug/L (or arrange IV ferric carboxymaltose infusion if oral intolerant or ferritin <30 ug/L)
Advise cessation of blood donations until ferritin >100 ug/L
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 53M regular blood donor presents with classic diagnostic criteria for Restless Legs Syndrome over 1 year, exacerbated by iron deficiency and OTC antihistamines.
reference_soap.objective: Neurological and vascular examination during daytime clinic: completely normal peripheral pulses, reflexes, sensation, and motor power (normal examination between evening attacks confirms primary RLS). Bloods: CRITICAL SCREENING for iron stores: check serum ferritin, iron panel, transferrin saturation, and FBC (ferritin <75 ug/L or transferrin saturation <20% strongly exacerbates central dopaminergic dysfunction in RLS even in the absence of overt anaemia; patient's regular blood donations cause depleted iron stores). Check U&Es (rule out uraemic RLS) and fasting glucose (peripheral neuropathy screen).
reference_soap.assessment: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom Disease) triggered/exacerbated by low brain/systemic iron stores from frequent blood donation and diphenhydramine use. DDx: peripheral neuropathy (continuous burning pain without strict evening/rest dependence or relief with movement), nocturnal leg cramps (sudden painful muscle contractions palpably tight), akathisia (neuroleptic-induced inner restlessness), vascular claudication.
reference_soap.plan: Stop over-the-counter diphenhydramine and review any prescribed medicines that may exacerbate symptoms with the prescriber. Check iron studies and treat iron deficiency according to local guidance; consider specialist input for oral or intravenous iron. Advise pausing blood donation until iron status has recovered. Recommend reducing late-day caffeine and alcohol, with evening stretching or warm baths. If symptoms persist, consider an alpha-2-delta ligand or other treatment with a clinician, accounting for adverse effects and augmentation risk.

learning_objectives: Apply the four cardinal diagnostic criteria of Restless Legs Syndrome (urge to move, rest induction, movement relief, evening/circadian worsening)
Identify central/systemic iron deficiency (serum ferritin <75 ug/L) as the primary reversible driver of dopaminergic dysfunction in RLS
Recognise common over-the-counter and prescription drug triggers that worsen RLS (sedating antihistamines, SSRIs, antiemetics)
Select alpha-2-delta ligands (pregabalin/gabapentin) over dopamine agonists as preferred first-line therapy to prevent augmentation syndrome

teaching.one_liner: An irresistible urge to move the legs with uncomfortable crawling sensations that strictly follow an evening/nighttime pattern and are relieved by movement — often linked to low iron stores, which frequent blood donation can cause.
red_flags: Constant, not evening-predominant, sensory symptoms — suggests peripheral neuropathy rather than RLS
Motor weakness or muscle wasting on exam — raises concern for a structural neuropathy or radiculopathy
Severe or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia — needs its own investigation and can exacerbate RLS

must_ask.say: Does this only happen in the evening or at night, when you're sitting or lying still?
Does getting up and moving around make it better?
How would you describe the feeling — crawling, fizzy, tingling?
How often do you donate blood?
How much is this affecting your sleep?

history.answer: I'm having terrible trouble sleeping because every evening my legs get this overwhelming urge to move and a creepy-crawly feeling in my calves.
It is mostly trouble falling asleep. I lie awake for hours because my legs won't stay still, leaving me with only about three hours of broken sleep.
This has been happening almost every single night for the past year.
There was no specific life event or stress that started it. It just reliably begins whenever I sit down to rest in the evening.
I get into bed around 10 PM and wake up at 6 AM, but it takes me hours to fall asleep. Weekends are the exact same struggle.
I feel exhausted and irritable all day long. My biggest fear is nodding off behind the wheel during my daily commute.
I don't take naps during the day. In the evening I watch TV from the couch, and in bed I find myself constantly checking the clock in frustration.
I drink two cups of coffee in the late afternoon to push through work. I do not drink alcohol to help me fall asleep.
My wife says I don't snore loudly or stop breathing, and I never wake up with morning headaches.
Yes, every evening between 8 PM and 10 PM when resting, I get an irresistible urge to move my legs. Pacing or stretching relieves it in seconds, but it returns as soon as I lie back down.
It feels like a crawling, fizzy, creeping sensation deep inside my calves and thighs, almost like worms wiggling under my skin.
No, I work regular daytime hours from nine to five as a software manager and never do night or shift work.
I am worn out and irritable from the lack of sleep, but I don't feel depressed or constantly anxious.
No, I have never had thoughts of harming myself or ending my life.
No, I have never had periods where I felt energetic or unusually euphoric on very little sleep; I am desperate for real rest.
I don't have night pain, shortness of breath, chest palpitations, or waking to urinate. My mild reflux is well controlled.
I tried taking an over-the-counter allergy sleeping pill, diphenhydramine, but it made the leg crawling and urge to move dramatically worse.
Our bedroom is quiet, dark, and cool, and I sleep with my wife.
My wife tells me that once I finally drift off, my legs twitch and kick repeatedly through the night.
I have been donating a unit of whole blood every three months for the last four years.
I wondered if sitting at an office desk all day caused poor circulation or restless veins in my legs.
I'm exhausted and really worried I might cause a car accident, so I was hoping for a sleeping pill or circulation medicine to stop the crawling.
Other than mild acid reflux, I've had no major health problems.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take omeprazole 20 milligrams once a day for acid reflux. I stopped the over-the-counter sleep medicine because it worsened my legs.
I have no known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I rarely drink, maybe one glass of wine on a special occasion.
I work as a software manager at an office desk, and I live with my wife.
No one in my family has had restless legs, movement issues, or chronic sleep disorders to my knowledge.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body mass index 24.2 kg/m2, neck circumference 38 cm.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted; sclerae are anicteric.
Normal oropharynx without tonsillar enlargement, airway crowding, or mucosal lesions.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, smooth, and without palpable nodules.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are bilaterally symmetric, strong, and regular.
Calves are soft, non-tender, and symmetric without swelling, cords, or warmth.
No pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.
Alert, oriented, mildly fatigued affect, with normal psychomotor activity and no overt anxiety.
Normal muscle bulk and tone; 5/5 strength throughout bilateral lower and upper extremities.
Intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in both legs without sensory level or neuropathy pattern.
Biceps, patellar, and Achilles reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; plantar responses are flexor.
